stem: You are a PGY1 on a rural placement in a general practice linked to a Yorke Peninsula hospital whose 4-bed emergency department is staffed overnight by one junior doctor with the GP on call. At 07:30 the practice nurse tells you that a 68-year-old man with metastatic lung cancer, known to the practice and receiving community palliative care, was found dead in bed by his wife this morning. His GP last reviewed him 6 days ago and had discussed that death was expected within weeks. The wife mentions that yesterday he fell down the back steps and hit his head but "seemed alright". She asks you to complete the paperwork so the funeral director can collect him. The GP is on the road and will arrive in an hour.
lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Complete the medical certificate of cause of death recording metastatic lung cancer, since death was expected.
Explain that the death must be reported to the Coroner because of the fall, and contact police or the State Coroner's Office before any certificate is issued.
Ask the community palliative care nurse to confirm the death so the funeral director can proceed.
Leave the body undisturbed and ask the wife to wait until the GP arrives to complete the certificate.

stem: A 32-year-old man is brought to the emergency department of a 30-bed Mid North regional hospital, 2 hours by road from Adelaide, after a witnessed first generalised tonic-clonic seizure at a roadhouse. He drives a B-double truck for a living and also drives his family car. He has recovered fully, examination is normal, blood glucose and electrolytes are normal, and he had no alcohol, drug use, head injury or sleep deprivation. CT is available in the morning and the physician on call advises outpatient neurology referral and EEG. He asks whether he can drive the truck back to the depot tomorrow, and whether he can at least drive his car in the meantime.
lead_in: Which statement best describes his driving status under the Austroads Assessing Fitness to Drive standards?

options.text: He may continue to drive the truck until neurology review, because a single seizure does not establish epilepsy.
He may drive his car but not the truck until a neurologist clears him for commercial driving.

He must not drive any vehicle now; the non-driving period after a first seizure is at least 6 months for a private licence and years for his commercial licence, and he is obliged to notify the Registrar.
He must stop driving both vehicle classes for 12 months and may then resume without specialist review.

stem: You are the junior doctor covering the ward and the emergency department overnight at a country hospital 90 minutes from the nearest tertiary centre. Earlier in the week you treated a 34-year-old woman for anaphylaxis to a wasp sting; she recovered fully and was discharged with an adrenaline autoinjector and an action plan. At 21:00 she comes to the emergency department desk with her partner and hands you an envelope containing $300 in cash "to say thank you for saving my life", plus a large box of chocolates for the nurses. The triage nurse is watching and the department is otherwise quiet. She is clearly emotional and says she will be offended if you refuse.
lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate response?

options.text: Accept the cash so as not to offend her, and declare it to the Director of Medical Services in the morning.
Accept the cash on the condition that it is shared among the nursing staff who were on duty.
Decline both the cash and the chocolates and explain that staff are not permitted to accept anything from patients.
Thank her warmly, decline the cash and explain that staff cannot accept money, and suggest a card or donation to the hospital; the shared chocolates may be accepted if local policy allows.

stem: You are the PGY1 on the medical ward of a metropolitan general hospital at 01:30. The medical registrar on site overnight has just arrived from the residents' room to review a 58-year-old man with new central chest pain, a heart rate of 104 and an ECG showing 1 mm ST depression in the lateral leads. As the registrar leans over the chart you notice a strong smell of alcohol, slurred speech and an unsteady gait; the registrar fumbles the ECG and says "just give him some morphine, he's fine". The nurse looks at you with concern. The on-call consultant physician is available by phone and there is an after-hours hospital coordinator in the building.
lead_in: What is the most appropriate action now?

options.text: Phone the on-call consultant immediately about both the patient and the registrar, and ensure the patient is managed by a doctor who is fit to practise.
Manage the patient yourself using the chest pain pathway and raise your concerns about the registrar with the Director of Clinical Training in the morning.
Ask the registrar to rest in the residents' room, cover the ward alone for the rest of the shift, and document what you observed.
Phone AHPRA now to make a mandatory notification, then continue the shift with the registrar once the call is made.

stem: You are a PGY2 on the general ward of a regional hospital with a small medical ward and no ICU. You and the intern are looking after a 55-year-old woman admitted with cellulitis, whose care has been thorough and appropriate. Over coffee the intern confides that he was diagnosed with depression 4 months ago, sees his GP monthly and a psychologist fortnightly, takes sertraline 100 mg daily, is sleeping well and feels he is coping at work. He asks you not to tell anyone. The ward nurse manager, who overheard part of the conversation, later asks you whether you now have to "report him to AHPRA".
lead_in: What is the most appropriate response to the nurse manager's question?

options.text: Yes, any mental illness in a registered practitioner must be notified to AHPRA within 30 days.
Yes, but the notification should be made through the Director of Clinical Training rather than directly.

No; a treated health condition that is not placing patients at substantial risk of harm does not meet the mandatory notification threshold, and the right response is to support him and encourage ongoing care.
No notification is needed provided he stops clinical duties until a psychiatrist confirms he is fit to work.

stem: You are the junior doctor covering the ward and emergency department overnight at a country hospital 90 minutes from the nearest tertiary centre; the GP is on call by phone. At 23:00 you treated a 38-year-old man with left renal colic, charting ketorolac 30 mg intramuscularly, which the nurse gave. At 01:00, while writing the discharge summary, you notice the triage alert sheet records an allergy to ibuprofen (generalised urticaria 5 years ago); you had not seen it and did not ask. Two hours after the dose he is comfortable, with no rash, wheeze or hypotension, and is asking to go home. The nurse asks what you want to do.
lead_in: What is the most appropriate course of action?

options.text: Complete an incident report in the Safety Learning System and let the GP on call decide in the morning whether the patient needs to be told, since no harm has occurred.
Tell him now what happened and apologise, explain the plan to observe him, phone the GP on call to inform them, and complete an incident report.
Observe him for a further 4 hours and disclose the error only if an allergic reaction develops, to avoid causing unnecessary anxiety.
Ask the nurse who administered the dose to tell him, because the administering clinician holds responsibility for the allergy check.

stem: You are a PGY2 covering the surgical ward and emergency department overnight at a country hospital 90 minutes from the nearest tertiary centre. A 55-year-old man is 2 days post open repair of an incisional hernia and has developed vomiting and abdominal distension. You phone the visiting surgeon, who is in Adelaide. The surgeon asks you to insert a nasogastric tube on free drainage, which you have done many times, and then to aspirate the tense fluid collection under the lower wound with a needle and syringe "to see if it is a seroma or a haematoma". You have never performed or observed aspiration of a wound collection. The surgeon will drive up in the morning.
lead_in: What is the most appropriate action?

options.text: Perform both procedures as instructed, because the surgeon has delegated them and carries responsibility for the outcome.
Decline both procedures until the surgeon can attend in person in the morning.
Watch an online video of wound aspiration and attempt it, documenting that it was done on the surgeon's instruction.
Insert the nasogastric tube, and tell the surgeon you are not trained in wound aspiration so that it is deferred or done under supervision.

stem: You are the junior doctor at a rural hospital on the Yorke Peninsula, where you staff the 4-bed emergency department alone overnight with the GP on call. Last week you treated a 52-year-old farmer for a deep laceration to his forearm from a shearing handpiece, which you closed and referred for review. Tonight a nurse shows you a post on the town's public community Facebook page in which he names you, describes his injury, the number of stitches and the tetanus booster, and thanks you for "saving the arm". He has also sent you a friend request. The nurse suggests you reply publicly "so people know the hospital is good" and that refusing the friend request would seem rude in a town this size.
lead_in: Which statement best describes your professional obligations in this situation?

options.text: You should not discuss his clinical details publicly even though he posted them himself, and should decline the friend request; a brief non-clinical thank you is acceptable.
Because he has disclosed the information himself, confidentiality no longer applies and you may reply with clinical reassurance about his recovery.
You should accept the friend request, because in a small community refusing would damage the therapeutic relationship.
You should ask the page administrator to remove his post because it breaches the hospital's social media policy.

stem: You are the PGY1 on the general ward of a 30-bed regional hospital in South Australia's Mid North, 2 hours by road from Adelaide. A 28-year-old man was admitted overnight with 18 hours of periumbilical pain that has moved to the right iliac fossa, anorexia and one vomit. On examination this morning his temperature is 37.9 degrees, heart rate 96, and he has localised tenderness with guarding at McBurney's point. Results: white cell count 14.2 x 10^9/L (neutrophils 11.5), CRP 62 mg/L, lipase normal, and urinalysis shows trace leucocytes with no nitrites or blood. The visiting surgeon is due at 10:00 and has asked you to phone with the results.
lead_in: Which interpretation of these findings is most accurate?

options.text: The urinary leucocytes indicate a urinary tract infection that explains his pain.
The absence of a temperature above 38 degrees makes appendicitis unlikely.
The history, examination and inflammatory markers are consistent with acute appendicitis; trace urinary leucocytes can occur when an inflamed appendix lies near the ureter or bladder.
The degree of leucocytosis indicates perforation and he should be transferred to Adelaide immediately.

stem: You are the PGY1 in the theatre suite of a tertiary hospital in Adelaide. A 58-year-old woman with adhesional small bowel obstruction after a previous hysterectomy has been booked for laparotomy; the surgical registrar has consented her and is scrubbing for the preceding case. The anaesthetist asks you to "get her ready". You find that she has been vomiting bilious fluid for 36 hours, no nasogastric tube has been inserted, group and hold has not been sent, and the potassium on this morning's bloods, which the registrar has not yet seen, is 2.9 mmol/L with a creatinine of 130 micromol/L. Her observations are stable. The anaesthetist expects to start in 45 minutes.
lead_in: Which task should you do first?

options.text: Take blood for group and hold and send it urgently.
Tell the anaesthetist and surgical registrar now that the potassium is 2.9 mmol/L and no nasogastric tube is in place.
Insert a nasogastric tube and connect it to free drainage.
Chart 40 mmol potassium chloride in 1 litre of sodium chloride 0.9% over 4 hours.

stem: You are the PGY1 covering the general ward overnight at a regional hospital with a small medical ward, no ICU, CT available only in business hours, and retrieval to Adelaide by road or air. A 70-year-old woman with a previous hysterectomy was admitted at 18:00 under the GP with vomiting and abdominal distension; an abdominal X-ray showed dilated small bowel loops, a nasogastric tube is draining, and she is on intravenous fluids awaiting surgical discussion in the morning. At 02:00 the nurse calls: she now has constant pain localised to the right lower abdomen with guarding, heart rate 118, blood pressure 95/60, temperature 38.2, and a venous lactate of 3.8 mmol/L. The GP on call is at home 15 minutes away.
lead_in: What is the most appropriate first action?

options.text: Request a repeat abdominal X-ray now and plan a CT when the department opens at 08:00.
Increase her analgesia, check the nasogastric tube is draining and review her at the morning ward round.
Start intravenous antibiotics and wait for the surgical registrar in Adelaide to call back after their morning handover.
Give a fluid bolus and call the GP on call now to arrange urgent surgical advice and retrieval.

stem: You are the PGY1 on the medical ward of a large metropolitan teaching hospital with on-site intensive care and 24-hour imaging. A 30-year-old Aboriginal woman from the APY Lands has a large left pleural effusion and the medical registrar plans a diagnostic pleural aspiration this afternoon. The registrar, who is in clinic, phones and asks you to "get the consent form signed" before 14:00. You have watched one pleural aspiration and have never performed one. The patient speaks Pitjantjatjara as her first language and conversational English, and she has asked whether her aunty can be with her and whether the Aboriginal Liaison Officer can come.
lead_in: Which statement about obtaining consent for this procedure is correct?

options.text: Consent should be obtained by a doctor able to perform the procedure or fully explain its risks and alternatives, usually the registrar; you can prepare her, arrange the interpreter and Aboriginal Liaison Officer, and welcome her aunty.
Any registered medical practitioner may obtain consent for any procedure, so you should complete the form now.
Consent is only valid if her family and the Aboriginal Liaison Officer are present when the form is signed.
The nurse in charge may obtain consent provided the registrar countersigns the form later.

stem: You are the junior doctor covering the surgical ward and emergency department overnight at a country hospital 90 minutes from the nearest tertiary centre. A 56-year-old man with type 2 diabetes on metformin has been admitted the evening before an elective open inguinal hernia repair under general anaesthesia, booked first on the list at 08:00 with the visiting surgeon and anaesthetist. He has no reflux, no gastroparesis and a body mass index of 29. At 20:00 the nurse tells you the ward's old "nil by mouth from midnight" sign is on his bed and asks what fasting instructions you want written up, because he is hungry and anxious about going hypoglycaemic overnight.
lead_in: What are the most appropriate fasting instructions?

options.text: Nothing by mouth, including water, from midnight.
A light meal until 2 hours before surgery and clear fluids until 30 minutes before.
A light meal until 6 hours before surgery (02:00) and clear fluids such as water or apple juice until 2 hours before (06:00).
Clear fluids only from 18:00 the evening before, then nothing after midnight.

stem: You are the PGY1 on the medical ward of a regional hospital with no ICU, CT in business hours only and retrieval to Adelaide. A 19-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes was admitted overnight with right iliac fossa pain and is booked for laparoscopic appendicectomy by the visiting surgeon. She has been fasting since midnight, received her usual insulin glargine last night, and has been on intravenous sodium chloride 0.9% without glucose. At 10:00 theatre tells you the list is running late and she will not go until about 14:00. The nurse reports her capillary glucose is 3.6 mmol/L; she feels shaky but is alert. The surgical consent is complete and the anaesthetist is in theatre.
lead_in: What should you do first?

options.text: Chart maintenance intravenous fluids containing 5% glucose and recheck the glucose in an hour.
Treat the hypoglycaemia now with oral glucose as a clear fluid or intravenous glucose, then inform the anaesthetist and surgeon of the result and the delay.
Withhold her next insulin glargine dose and extend the fast until the new theatre time is confirmed.
Give her a sandwich now and tell theatre she will need to be rebooked for tomorrow.

stem: You are a PGY2 on the general ward of a country hospital 90 minutes from the nearest tertiary centre. A 62-year-old man with permanent atrial fibrillation on apixaban 5 mg twice daily (CHA2DS2-VA score 2, no previous stroke, no mechanical valve) has been admitted 2 days before a transurethral resection of the prostate with the visiting urologist, who has asked that his anticoagulation be "sorted out" before the morning of surgery. His creatinine is 85 micromol/L, estimated creatinine clearance 80 mL/min, and his platelet count and haemoglobin are normal. The anaesthetist will see him tomorrow. He asks whether he should take tonight's dose.
lead_in: What is the most appropriate plan for his apixaban?

options.text: Continue apixaban through the perioperative period because the procedure is endoscopic and minor.
Stop apixaban 5 days before surgery and bridge with therapeutic enoxaparin until the night before.
Stop apixaban 24 hours before surgery.
Stop apixaban 48 hours before surgery with no bridging, and confirm the plan with the anaesthetist and urologist.

stem: You are a PGY2 on the medical ward of a 30-bed regional hospital in South Australia's Mid North, 2 hours by road from Adelaide, where the visiting surgeon operated yesterday and has now returned to Adelaide; the physician is available by phone. At 22:00 the nurse asks you to review a 34-year-old woman who is 18 hours post laparoscopic appendicectomy for uncomplicated appendicitis. Her temperature is 38.1 degrees, heart rate 92, blood pressure 118/74, respiratory rate 18 and oxygen saturation 97% on room air. She says she feels "a bit sore but okay", has passed urine, has a peripheral cannula in her left hand and received a single dose of cefazolin at induction.
lead_in: What is the most appropriate first step?

options.text: Examine her, including chest, port sites, cannula site, calves and abdomen, before deciding on investigations.
Start intravenous piperacillin-tazobactam now and take blood cultures once the first dose is running.
Arrange transfer to Adelaide tonight for CT of the abdomen to exclude an intra-abdominal collection.
Give paracetamol and ask the nurse to repeat the observations at the morning ward round.

stem: You are the PGY1 on the medical ward of a 30-bed regional hospital in South Australia's Mid North, 2 hours by road from Adelaide, with a visiting surgeon and specialist advice by phone. A 55-year-old woman is 5 days post open abdominal hysterectomy for fibroids. Her indwelling catheter was removed on day 2 and she has been voiding normally. This morning she has a temperature of 38.6 degrees with a rigor overnight, heart rate 105, blood pressure 112/70, respiratory rate 18 and saturations 97% on room air. The lower half of her wound is red, warm and tender with a 3 cm area of purulent discharge; the chest is clear; calves are soft; urinalysis shows trace leucocytes and no nitrites. White cell count is 16 x 10^9/L.
lead_in: What is the most likely cause of her fever?

options.text: Postoperative atelectasis
Catheter-associated urinary tract infection
Surgical site infection of the wound
Drug fever from the perioperative antibiotic

stem: You are the PGY1 covering the recovery and surgical ward area overnight at a country hospital 90 minutes from the nearest tertiary centre. A 30-year-old man had a laparotomy yesterday for a perforated appendix with washout; he is on a morphine patient-controlled analgesia pump, has a nasogastric tube that the surgeon removed this evening, and is nil by mouth. The nurse tells you he has a distended, quiet abdomen and has not passed flatus, and asks whether anything can be done to "get his bowels going" faster. The visiting surgeon is in Adelaide and has asked you to manage him overnight according to standard postoperative principles.
lead_in: Which measure is best supported for reducing the duration of postoperative ileus?

options.text: Reinserting the nasogastric tube and keeping it on free drainage until flatus is passed.
Opioid-sparing multimodal analgesia with early oral intake and mobilisation.
Regular intravenous metoclopramide for 72 hours.
Keeping him strictly nil by mouth with intravenous fluids until bowel sounds return.

stem: You are the junior doctor covering the recovery and surgical ward area of a tertiary hospital in Adelaide. A 70-year-old man, 6 hours post total hip replacement under spinal anaesthesia with sedation, is on a morphine patient-controlled analgesia pump (1 mg bolus, 5 minute lockout) and also received oxycodone 10 mg orally in recovery for breakthrough pain. The nurse asks you to review him: his sedation score is 2 (easy to rouse but unable to stay awake), respiratory rate 8 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 94% on 2 L nasal oxygen, blood pressure 128/76, heart rate 72 and pain score 2 out of 10. He has mild chronic kidney disease. The anaesthetic registrar is available by phone.
lead_in: Which interpretation of these observations is most accurate?

options.text: Pain is well controlled and the observations are acceptable for a patient recovering from anaesthesia.
The low respiratory rate reflects residual sedation from the anaesthetic and will resolve if the PCA continues with oxygen.
He is likely hypovolaemic from surgical blood loss, which explains his drowsiness.
He has opioid-induced ventilatory impairment; the sedation score is the key early sign, and the PCA should be stopped and the anaesthetic registrar called.

stem: You are a PGY2 covering the general ward of a 30-bed regional hospital in South Australia's Mid North, 2 hours by road from Adelaide. A 50-year-old woman had an open inguinal hernia repair under spinal anaesthesia at 10:00; the visiting anaesthetist and surgeon have left and are available by phone. At 18:00 the nurse reports she has not passed urine since the morning, received 2 litres of intravenous fluid during and after surgery, is uncomfortable with a palpable suprapubic mass, and the bladder scan shows 650 mL. Sensation in her legs has fully returned. She has no history of urinary problems and her creatinine was normal preoperatively. She has tried voiding in the shower without success.
lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Catheterise her now, leaving an indwelling catheter with a plan for a trial of void within 24 hours.
Give a further litre of intravenous fluid, encourage voiding in a warm shower and rescan in 2 hours.
Prescribe tamsulosin tonight and reassess her ability to void at the morning ward round.
Withhold catheterisation and ask the surgeon by phone whether it is contraindicated after an inguinal hernia repair.

stem: You are a PGY2 on the general ward of a metropolitan general hospital with a busy medical ward and a registrar on site overnight. A 58-year-old woman was admitted this evening for a laparoscopic cholecystectomy on tomorrow morning's list after two episodes of biliary colic; she was seen in pre-admission clinic 3 weeks ago and cleared. While clerking her you learn that over the past fortnight she has had central chest tightness walking up the ramp from the car park, settling within minutes of rest, with no pain at rest. She has hypertension and smokes 15 cigarettes a day. Her admission ECG shows new T-wave inversion in V4 to V6 compared with the pre-admission tracing. She is currently pain free with normal observations.
lead_in: What is the most appropriate action?

options.text: Proceed as planned, because the symptoms are stable and lateral T-wave changes are non-specific.
Request an outpatient stress echocardiogram after discharge and allow the surgery to proceed in the morning.
Inform the anaesthetist and surgical registrar tonight of the new symptoms and ECG changes, send a troponin, and expect surgery to be deferred for cardiology assessment.
Start aspirin and a beta blocker tonight so that the operation can go ahead safely in the morning.

stem: You are the PGY1 on the general ward of a metropolitan general hospital with a registrar on site overnight. A 29-year-old woman has been admitted the night before an elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy under general anaesthesia. She is otherwise well, takes no regular medications, has no family history of bleeding or anaesthetic problems, does not smoke, and has a normal examination with a body mass index of 24. Her last menstrual period was 5 weeks ago and she says her periods are sometimes irregular. The anaesthetist has asked you to make sure the "routine preoperative tests" are done before the morning and the nurse asks which forms to prepare.
lead_in: Which preoperative test is indicated for this patient?

options.text: Chest X-ray
Urine or serum pregnancy test
Resting 12-lead ECG
Coagulation screen

stem: You are the PGY1 covering the surgical ward of a metropolitan general hospital overnight; the surgical registrar is on site. A 78-year-old man is 2 days post anterior resection for rectal cancer with a pelvic drain that has been producing about 50 mL of serosanguineous fluid per shift. At 03:00 the nurse calls you: over the last 2 hours the drain has filled with 400 mL of frank blood, his heart rate is 112, blood pressure 98/58, respiratory rate 22 and he is pale and anxious. He takes aspirin, which was restarted this morning, and his haemoglobin yesterday was 102 g/L. He has one 20-gauge cannula in situ.
lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Clamp the drain to tamponade the bleeding and reassess the output in an hour.
Remove the drain, as it may be eroding a vessel, and apply a firm dressing over the site.
Give a litre of sodium chloride 0.9%, order one unit of red cells and review at the morning ward round.
Call the surgical registrar now, insert a second large-bore cannula, send a group and crossmatch and full blood count, and leave the drain unclamped.

stem: You are a PGY2 on the general ward of a metropolitan general hospital with a registrar on site overnight. A 22-year-old man is 3 days post open appendicectomy for a perforated appendix and has received intravenous amoxicillin-clavulanate since surgery. Overnight he developed severe pain around the wound that the nurse describes as out of proportion to the appearance, needing repeated opioid doses. On examination at 05:00 he is confused and sweaty, temperature 39.4 degrees, heart rate 128, blood pressure 102/60. The wound edges show faint dusky erythema with a thin grey, foul-smelling discharge; the tenderness and induration extend well beyond the erythema, and you feel crepitus in the right flank. Bloods: white cell count 24 x 10^9/L, CRP 310 mg/L, sodium 128 mmol/L, creatinine 150 micromol/L, lactate 4.1 mmol/L.
lead_in: Which interpretation of these findings is most accurate?

options.text: A necrotising soft tissue infection of the abdominal wall; this is a surgical emergency needing immediate surgical review for debridement alongside sepsis management.
A superficial incisional surgical site infection; the wound should be opened, swabbed and treated with oral antibiotics.
An intra-abdominal collection; a CT with percutaneous drainage will address the fever and the wound changes are incidental.
Cellulitis around the wound; intravenous flucloxacillin and marking the erythema for reassessment in 12 hours are appropriate.

stem: You are the PGY1 assisting in the pre-admission clinic and theatre suite of a 30-bed regional hospital in South Australia's Mid North, 2 hours by road from Adelaide, where the visiting surgeon runs a monthly list. A 55-year-old woman, weight 78 kg, with no drug allergies and no history of multi-resistant organisms, is booked for an elective open repair of an umbilical hernia with mesh under general anaesthesia tomorrow. The anaesthetist asks you to chart her surgical antibiotic prophylaxis on the medication chart so the theatre nurse can prepare it, and to note when it should be given.
lead_in: What is the correct prophylactic antibiotic regimen?

options.text: Cefalexin 500 mg orally with breakfast on the morning of surgery.
Cefazolin 2 g intravenously at skin incision, then 8-hourly for 24 hours.
Cefazolin 2 g intravenously as a single dose within 60 minutes before skin incision.
Cefazolin 2 g intravenously in recovery after wound closure.
